claim: LiGluN2A(V713C) co-expressed with wildtype GluN1a generates an inward current when illuminated with 380 nm light in HEK293 cells.

claim: The speed of MAG photoswitching depends on light intensity.
source: MAG photoswitching provides two advantageous properties for the remote control of NMDA receptors. First, since the speed of MAG photoswitching depends on light intensity so that switching can be achieved either with short high intensity pulses or longer low intensity pulses (Gorostiza et al., 2007; Reiner and Isacoff, 2014), it should be possible to sculpt the photocurrent to resemble NMDA receptor excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCNMDA).

evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1f, with citations.

claim: Widefield photoactivation at 380 nm of both LiGluN2A and LiGluN2B triggered an increase in EPSC frequency.
source: Widefield photoactivation at 380 nm of both LiGluN2A and LiGluN2B triggered an increase in EPSC frequency and this was reversed—more slowly in LiGluN2B—by illumination at 510 nm (Figure 2c), suggesting that photoactivation of NMDA receptors containing either LiGluN2A or LiGluN2B triggered action potential firing in presynaptic neurons.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Photoactivation of NMDA receptors containing either LiGluN2A or LiGluN2B triggered action potential firing in presynaptic neurons.
source: Widefield photoactivation at 380 nm of both LiGluN2A and LiGluN2B triggered an increase in EPSC frequency and this was reversed—more slowly in LiGluN2B—by illumination at 510 nm (Figure 2c), suggesting that photoactivation of NMDA receptors containing either LiGluN2A or LiGluN2B triggered action potential firing in presynaptic neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that photoactivation triggered an increase in EPSC frequency.

claim: Photoactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster rise of excitation than LiGluN2B.
source: Photoactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster rise of excitation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, top insets, and f) and photodeactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster (~three fold) de-excitation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, bottom insets, and g) than neurons expressing LiGluN2B.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, top insets, and f.

claim: Photodeactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster (~three fold) de-excitation than neurons expressing LiGluN2B.
source: Photoactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster rise of excitation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, top insets, and f) and photodeactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster (~three fold) de-excitation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, bottom insets, and g) than neurons expressing LiGluN2B.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, bottom insets, and g.

claim: The largest photo-antagonism was generated by L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit when expressed in hippocampal neurons.
source: The largest photo-antagonism was generated by L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit when expressed in hippocampal neurons (56.4 ± 2.9% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA, n = 7) (Figure 3b, c and f), similar to the block observed in HEK293 cells (65.8 ± 4.3% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate in HEK cells, n = 9).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3b, c and f.

claim: L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit produces 56.4 ± 2.9% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA in hippocampal neurons.
source: The largest photo-antagonism was generated by L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit when expressed in hippocampal neurons (56.4 ± 2.9% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA, n = 7) (Figure 3b, c and f), similar to the block observed in HEK293 cells (65.8 ± 4.3% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate in HEK cells, n = 9).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3b, c and f.

claim: L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit produces 65.8 ± 4.3% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate in HEK293 cells.
source: The largest photo-antagonism was generated by L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit when expressed in hippocampal neurons (56.4 ± 2.9% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA, n = 7) (Figure 3b, c and f), similar to the block observed in HEK293 cells (65.8 ± 4.3% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate in HEK cells, n = 9).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3b, c and f.

claim: Photo-antagonism of GluN2A by L-MAG0 at G712C is on par with the antagonism of GluN2A by NVP-AAM077 when applied at concentrations that maintain subunit selectivity.
source: This photo-antagonism is on par with the antagonism of GluN2A by NVP-AAM077, when applied at concentrations that maintain subunit selectivity (Monaghan et al., 2012; Neyton and Paoletti, 2006; Paoletti and Neyton, 2007), and so, although incomplete (likely due to labeling efficiency, see below and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), would be predicted to have utility.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data with published data and is supported by citations.

claim: A screen of cysteine mutants around the glycine-binding pocket of GluN1 identified a labeling site, E406C, where L-MAG0 functioned as photo-antagonist.
source: Indeed, a screen of cysteine mutants around the glycine-binding pocket identified a labeling site, E406C, where L-MAG0 functioned as photo-antagonist (30.7 ± 1.7% inhibition of the total current neurons, n = 6) (Figure 3b, d and f), without affecting the glycine potency of the subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3b, d and f.

claim: L-MAG0 at E406C of GluN1a produces 30.7 ± 1.7% inhibition of the total current in neurons.
source: Indeed, a screen of cysteine mutants around the glycine-binding pocket identified a labeling site, E406C, where L-MAG0 functioned as photo-antagonist (30.7 ± 1.7% inhibition of the total current neurons, n = 6) (Figure 3b, d and f), without affecting the glycine potency of the subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3b, d and f.

claim: L-MAG0 at E406C of GluN1a does not affect the glycine potency of the subunit.
source: Indeed, a screen of cysteine mutants around the glycine-binding pocket identified a labeling site, E406C, where L-MAG0 functioned as photo-antagonist (30.7 ± 1.7% inhibition of the total current neurons, n = 6) (Figure 3b, d and f), without affecting the glycine potency of the subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f.

claim: Co-expression of GluN1a(E406C) and GluN2A(G712C) in dissociated hippocampal neurons and incubation with L-MAG0 resulted in 73.8 ± 5.2% photo-inhibition of the total NMDA-induced current.
source: When the photo-antagonizable GluN1a(E406C) and GluN2A(G712C) subunits were co-expressed in dissociated hippocampal neurons and incubated with L-MAG0, their combined effect resulted in 73.8 ± 5.2% (n = 4) photo-inhibition of the total NMDA-induced current in neurons (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3e,f.

claim: Photo-antagonism with 370 nm light hyperpolarized cells and suppressed firing in cultured hippocampal neurons transfected with GluN2A(G712C) and GluN1a(E406C) and labeled with L-MAG0.
source: Cultured hippocampal neurons from wt rats (C57BL) transfected with the photo-antagonizing GluN2A(G712C) subunit in combination with photo-antagonizing GluN1a(E406C), labeled with L-MAG0 and under green light illumination, exhibited typical action potential activity under current clamp recordings. Photo-antagonism with 370 nm light hyperpolarized cells and suppressed firing (Figure 4a,b), as seen with conventional NMDA receptor blockers.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: No photo-effect was seen in non-transfected cells labeled with L-MAG0.
source: No such photo-effect was seen in non-transfected cells (Figure 4c,d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4c,d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reversal of photo-antagonism by 510 nm light elicited a gradual repolarization.
source: Reversal of photo-antagonism by 510 nm light elicited a gradual repolarization, reminiscent of physiological recovery (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Illumination with violet light decreased the inward current, the frequency of action currents, and of spontaneous EPSCNMDA in neurons transfected with GluN2A(G712C) alone, or in combination with GluN1a(E406C).
source: In voltage clamp, neurons transfected with the photo-antagonizing GluN2A(G712C) subunit alone, or in combination with the photo-antagonizing GluN1a(E406C), displayed typical barrages of spontaneous EPSCNMDAevents (Groc et al., 2002; Ivenshitz and Segal, 2010; Kirson and Yaari, 1996) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a). During green light illumination, action currents were detected in some cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, arrow and inset) and illumination with violet light decreased the inward current, the frequency of action currents (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, inset), and of spontaneous EPSCNMDA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, and summary in d), with no effect of violet light on non-transfected neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, right panel, summary in c and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, with citations.

claim: Violet light had no effect on non-transfected neurons.
source: In voltage clamp, neurons transfected with the photo-antagonizing GluN2A(G712C) subunit alone, or in combination with the photo-antagonizing GluN1a(E406C), displayed typical barrages of spontaneous EPSCNMDAevents (Groc et al., 2002; Ivenshitz and Segal, 2010; Kirson and Yaari, 1996) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a). During green light illumination, action currents were detected in some cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, arrow and inset) and illumination with violet light decreased the inward current, the frequency of action currents (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, inset), and of spontaneous EPSCNMDA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, and summary in d), with no effect of violet light on non-transfected neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, right panel, summary in c and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, right panel, summary in c and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Transfected neurons that formed autapses displayed eEPSCNMDA events that were similar in amplitude and kinetics to those seen in non-transfected cells.
source: Transfected neurons that formed autapses displayed eEPSCNMDA events that were similar in amplitude and kinetics to those seen in non-transfected cells (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), indicating that LiGluN expression makes synaptic NMDA receptors sensitive to light without significantly changing their number, consistent with evidence presented above (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d) and with earlier reports which expressed wildtype subunits (Prybylowski et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, with a citation.

claim: LiGluN expression makes synaptic NMDA receptors sensitive to light without significantly changing their number.
source: Transfected neurons that formed autapses displayed eEPSCNMDA events that were similar in amplitude and kinetics to those seen in non-transfected cells (Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), indicating that LiGluN expression makes synaptic NMDA receptors sensitive to light without significantly changing their number, consistent with evidence presented above (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d) and with earlier reports which expressed wildtype subunits (Prybylowski et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that transfected neurons displayed eEPSCNMDA events similar to non-transfected cells.

claim: In neurons transfected with LiGluN2A(G712C) and labeled with L-MAG0, the amplitude of the eEPSCNMDA was inhibited by illumination at 370 nm and this photo-antagonism was relieved by illumination at 510 nm.
source: In neurons that were transfected with the photo-antagonizing LiGluN2A(G712C) and labeled with L-MAG0, the amplitude of the eEPSCNMDA was inhibited by illumination at 370 nm and this photo-antagonism was relieved by illumination at 510 nm (Figure 5c, d and f).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5c, d and f.

claim: The photo-antagonism of eEPSCNMDA could be toggled on and off repeatedly.
source: The photo-antagonism could be toggled on and off repeatedly (Figure 5c,d), whereas non-transfected neurons showed no change in their eEPSCNMDA's amplitude as the wavelength of illumination was switched between 510 nm and 370 nm (Figure 5e,f).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: Non-transfected neurons showed no change in their eEPSCNMDA's amplitude as the wavelength of illumination was switched between 510 nm and 370 nm.
source: The photo-antagonism could be toggled on and off repeatedly (Figure 5c,d), whereas non-transfected neurons showed no change in their eEPSCNMDA's amplitude as the wavelength of illumination was switched between 510 nm and 370 nm (Figure 5e,f).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5e,f.

claim: The magnitude of the light-dependent inhibition of the synaptic eEPSCNMDA was not correlated with eEPSCNMDA amplitude.
source: The magnitude of the light-dependent inhibition of the synaptic eEPSCNMDA was not correlated with eEPSCNMDA amplitude, suggesting that the degree of inhibition varies primarily with labeling efficiency (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b; % inhibition ranges from ~20-50%), but also see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The degree of inhibition of eEPSCNMDA varies primarily with labeling efficiency.
source: The magnitude of the light-dependent inhibition of the synaptic eEPSCNMDA was not correlated with eEPSCNMDA amplitude, suggesting that the degree of inhibition varies primarily with labeling efficiency (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b; % inhibition ranges from ~20-50%), but also see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the magnitude of inhibition was not correlated with eEPSCNMDA amplitude.

claim: LiGluN subunits incorporate into synaptic NMDA receptors and function normally in response to synaptically released glutamate.
source: Thus, LiGluN subunits incorporate into synaptic NMDA receptors and function normally in response to synaptically released glutamate, while providing for optical control over the synaptic transmission that is mediated by that specific receptor subtype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings reported in the results section.

claim: Organotypic slices from GluN2A-knockout neonate mice were biolistically transfected with GluN1a(E406C), GluN2A(G712C) and tdTomato.
source: Organotypic slices from GluN2A-knockout neonate mice (Sakimura et al., 1995) were biolistically transfected with GluN1a(E406C), GluN2A(G712C) and tdTomato (typically 1–3 transfected CA1 neurons per slice, Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure and is shown in Figure 6b, with a citation.

claim: Slices in which L-MAG0 was maintained in trans (photo-antagonism off) by green light exhibited robust LTP.
source: Slices, in which L-MAG0 was maintained in trans (photo-antagonism off) by green light, exhibited robust LTP (Figure 6c, black circles; EPSC amplitude increased to 185 + 31% (n = 10) of baseline, averaged over 20–30 min. post-tetanus; summary in Figure 6d), whereas slices in which L-MAG0 was switched to cis (photo-antagonism on) by violet light did not (Figure 6c, open circles; EPSC amplitude dropped to 67 + 28% (n = 10) of baseline, averaged over 20–30 min. post-tetanus; summary in Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6c and 6d.

claim: Slices in which L-MAG0 was switched to cis (photo-antagonism on) by violet light did not exhibit LTP.
source: Slices, in which L-MAG0 was maintained in trans (photo-antagonism off) by green light, exhibited robust LTP (Figure 6c, black circles; EPSC amplitude increased to 185 + 31% (n = 10) of baseline, averaged over 20–30 min. post-tetanus; summary in Figure 6d), whereas slices in which L-MAG0 was switched to cis (photo-antagonism on) by violet light did not (Figure 6c, open circles; EPSC amplitude dropped to 67 + 28% (n = 10) of baseline, averaged over 20–30 min. post-tetanus; summary in Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6c and 6d.

claim: Slices to which L-MAG0 was not added, but which were illuminated at 390 nm, exhibited the same level of LTP as those labeled with L-MAG0 and illuminated with 497 nm light.
source: Slices to which L-MAG0 was not added, but which were illuminated at 390 nm, exhibited the same level of LTP as those labeled with L-MAG0 and illuminated with 497 nm light (174 + 31.74%, n = 4), demonstrating that the light protocol did not interfere with the generation of LTP and that the block of LTP-induction is a specific outcome of photo-antagonism.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section that demonstrates the specificity of the photo-antagonism effect.

claim: The light protocol did not interfere with the generation of LTP.
source: Slices to which L-MAG0 was not added, but which were illuminated at 390 nm, exhibited the same level of LTP as those labeled with L-MAG0 and illuminated with 497 nm light (174 + 31.74%, n = 4), demonstrating that the light protocol did not interfere with the generation of LTP and that the block of LTP-induction is a specific outcome of photo-antagonism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that slices without L-MAG0 exhibited LTP when illuminated at 390 nm.

claim: The block of LTP-induction is a specific outcome of photo-antagonism.
source: Slices to which L-MAG0 was not added, but which were illuminated at 390 nm, exhibited the same level of LTP as those labeled with L-MAG0 and illuminated with 497 nm light (174 + 31.74%, n = 4), demonstrating that the light protocol did not interfere with the generation of LTP and that the block of LTP-induction is a specific outcome of photo-antagonism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that slices without L-MAG0 exhibited LTP when illuminated at 390 nm.

claim: Photo-antagonism of post-synaptic NMDA receptors can be used to gate the induction of LTP that is induced by presynaptic bursts of action potentials.
source: Thus, photo-antagonism of post-synaptic NMDA receptors can be used to gate the induction of LTP that is induced by presynaptic bursts of action potentials.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings reported in the results section.

claim: Illumination of a single spine head at 405 nm elicited a rise in R-GECO fluorescence in the illuminated spine, with little or no response in nearby spines or in the dendritic shaft.
source: Illumination of a single spine head at 405 nm (100 µW for 100 µs/pixel) elicited a rise in R-GECO fluorescence in the illuminated spine, with little or no response in nearby spines or in the dendritic shaft, consistent with spine head Ca2+-signaling compartmentalization (Figure 7b,c) (Yuste, 2013).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7b,c, with a citation.

claim: Spine head illumination with 405 nm triggered an increase in spine head volume that peaked in ~5 min.
source: Spine head illumination with 405 nm (100 µW/µm2 for 600 μs per pixel, ~200 ms per spine) triggered an increase in spine head volume that peaked in ~5 min (Ft/Fi = 1.67 ± 0.15 of baseline, n = 26, p<0.001, two-tailed, paired t-test) and then declined to an elevated plateau that persisted for at least 45 min (Ft/Fi = 1.31 ± 0.06 of baseline, n = 26, p<0.001, two-tailed, paired t-test) (Figure 7d and e, red symbols).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7d and e.

claim: Spine head volume declined to an elevated plateau that persisted for at least 45 min after photo-activation.
source: Spine head illumination with 405 nm (100 µW/µm2 for 600 μs per pixel, ~200 ms per spine) triggered an increase in spine head volume that peaked in ~5 min (Ft/Fi = 1.67 ± 0.15 of baseline, n = 26, p<0.001, two-tailed, paired t-test) and then declined to an elevated plateau that persisted for at least 45 min (Ft/Fi = 1.31 ± 0.06 of baseline, n = 26, p<0.001, two-tailed, paired t-test) (Figure 7d and e, red symbols).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7d and e.

claim: Non-illuminated nearby spines did not change volume.
source: Non-illuminated nearby spines did not change volume (Figure 7e, black symbols), nor did illuminated spines in slices that were not labeled with L-MAG1 (Figure 7d and e, blue symbols).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Illuminated spines in slices that were not labeled with L-MAG1 did not change volume.
source: Non-illuminated nearby spines did not change volume (Figure 7e, black symbols), nor did illuminated spines in slices that were not labeled with L-MAG1 (Figure 7d and e, blue symbols).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7d and e.

claim: LiGluN2A(V713C) traffics to synapses.
source: These experiments show that: i) LiGluN2A(V713C) traffics to synapses, as shown above for LiGluN2A(G712C), ii) photo-agonism of GluN2A(V713C) can be used to induce a spine-specific elevation in internal calcium, and iii) activation of post-synaptic GluN2A-containing receptors is sufficient to induce the morphological correlate of LTP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings reported in the results section.

claim: Photo-agonism of GluN2A(V713C) can be used to induce a spine-specific elevation in internal calcium.
source: These experiments show that: i) LiGluN2A(V713C) traffics to synapses, as shown above for LiGluN2A(G712C), ii) photo-agonism of GluN2A(V713C) can be used to induce a spine-specific elevation in internal calcium, and iii) activation of post-synaptic GluN2A-containing receptors is sufficient to induce the morphological correlate of LTP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings reported in the results section.

claim: Activation of post-synaptic GluN2A-containing receptors is sufficient to induce the morphological correlate of LTP.
source: These experiments show that: i) LiGluN2A(V713C) traffics to synapses, as shown above for LiGluN2A(G712C), ii) photo-agonism of GluN2A(V713C) can be used to induce a spine-specific elevation in internal calcium, and iii) activation of post-synaptic GluN2A-containing receptors is sufficient to induce the morphological correlate of LTP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings reported in the results section.

claim: The first uncaging bout, during GluN1a/GluN2A photo-antagonism, induced only a small, transient increase in spine head volume.
source: The first uncaging bout, during GluN1a/GluN2A photo-antagonism, induced only a small, transient increase in spine head volume, which peaked in 1 min (Ft/Fi = 1.18 ± 0.07 of baseline, n = 12, p>0.1, two tailed, paired t-test) and shrank back to near baseline (Ft/Fi F = 1.05 ± 0.05 of baseline, n = 12, p>0.1, two tailed, paired t-test) within 5 min (Figure 8c, red symbols), indicating a lack of the long-lasting expansion that is associated with LTP (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 8c, with a citation.

claim: After turning off the GluN1a/GluN2A photo-antagonism with green light, the second bout of near-spine glutamate uncaging induced a large persistent expansion.
source: After turning off the GluN1a/GluN2A photo-antagonism with green light, the second bout of near-spine glutamate uncaging induced a large persistent expansion (Ft/Fi = 1.47 ± 0.13 compared to new moderately elevated baseline between t = 3 min and 15 min, n = 12, p<0.01, two tailed, paired t-test) (Figure 8c, red symbols).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Nearby, non-illuminated spines did not respond to glutamate uncaging.
source: Nearby, non-illuminated spines did not respond (Figure 8b and c, black symbols).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 8b and c.

claim: Photo-antagonism of GluN1a/GluN2A can block the induction of spine expansion and this block is reversible.
source: These experiments show that photo-antagonism of GluN1a/GluN2A can block the induction of spine expansion and that this block is reversible, enabling a morphological correlate of LTP to be gated temporally at single synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings reported in the results section.

claim: A transgenic line of zebrafish expressing GluN2A(G712C) under the control the gal4-UAS expression system was generated.
source: We generated a transgenic line of zebrafish expressing GluN2A(G712C) under the control the gal4-UAS expression system (Scott et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure and is supported by a citation.

claim: At 5.25 dpf, the size distribution of retinal ganglion cell axon arbors from Tg[s1101t-gal4;UAS-GluN2A(G712C)] larvae was indistinguishable that of siblings lacking the UAS-GluN2A(G712C) transgene.
source: At 5.25 dpf (126 ± 2 hr post fertilization), the size distribution of retinal ganglion cell axon arbors from Tg[s1101t-gal4;UAS-GluN2A(G712C)] larvae was indistinguishable that of siblings lacking the UAS-GluN2A(G712C) transgene (Figure 9d) (p>0.7, two- two-tailed, unpaired t-test, n = 19 Tg[s1101t-gal4;UAS-GluN2A(G712C)] and n = 10 control axons), indicating that gal4-driven expression of UAS-GluN2A(G712C) does not alter the initial development of the retinotectal projection.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 9d.

claim: Gal4-driven expression of UAS-GluN2A(G712C) does not alter the initial development of the retinotectal projection.
source: At 5.25 dpf (126 ± 2 hr post fertilization), the size distribution of retinal ganglion cell axon arbors from Tg[s1101t-gal4;UAS-GluN2A(G712C)] larvae was indistinguishable that of siblings lacking the UAS-GluN2A(G712C) transgene (Figure 9d) (p>0.7, two- two-tailed, unpaired t-test, n = 19 Tg[s1101t-gal4;UAS-GluN2A(G712C)] and n = 10 control axons), indicating that gal4-driven expression of UAS-GluN2A(G712C) does not alter the initial development of the retinotectal projection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that the size distribution of axon arbors was indistinguishable between transgenic and control larvae.

claim: By 7 dpf, axon arbors in Tg[s1101t-gal4;UAS-GluN2A(G712C)] larvae that were illuminated episodically to induce photo-antagonism showed a significant increase in arbor radius.
source: However, by 7 dpf, axon arbors in Tg[s1101t-gal4;UAS-GluN2A(G712C)] larvae that were illuminated episodically to induce photo-antagonism showed a significant increase in arbor radius (Figure 9f, ΔR = 16.4 ± 1.7%, n = 12 axons), compared to illuminated vehicle-treated (ΔR = 1.2 ± 3.4%, n = 9 axons) or wild-type siblings (ΔR = 6.9% ± 2.6%, n = 10 axons) (Figure 9—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 9f.

claim: Tg[s1101t-gal4;UAS-GluN2A(G712C)] larvae that were not treated with MAG, but were instead reared in 25 µM MK-801, showed a comparable increase in arbor radius to those treated with MAG and illuminated.
source: Tg[s1101t-gal4;UAS-GluN2A(G712C)] larvae that were not treated with MAG, but were instead reared in 25 µM MK-801, under the same conditions from 5–7 dpf, showed a comparable increase in arbor radius (ΔR = 13.8 ± 3.7%, n = 10 axons), indicating that the efficacy of photo-antagonism was on par with a relatively strong dose of a soluble NMDA receptor blocker.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section that demonstrates the efficacy of photo-antagonism.

claim: The efficacy of photo-antagonism was on par with a relatively strong dose of a soluble NMDA receptor blocker.
source: Tg[s1101t-gal4;UAS-GluN2A(G712C)] larvae that were not treated with MAG, but were instead reared in 25 µM MK-801, under the same conditions from 5–7 dpf, showed a comparable increase in arbor radius (ΔR = 13.8 ± 3.7%, n = 10 axons), indicating that the efficacy of photo-antagonism was on par with a relatively strong dose of a soluble NMDA receptor blocker.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of photo-antagonism with MK-801 treatment.

claim: MAG treatment alone had no effect on development compared to vehicle-treated siblings, based on an assessment of spontaneous swim behavior, escape behavior and habituation of escape behavior.
source: MAG treatment alone had no effect on development compared to vehicle-treated siblings, based on an assessment of spontaneous swim behavior, escape behavior and habituation of escape behavior (Figure 9—figure supplement 1b and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Extended photo-antagonism of LiGluN2A(G712C) mimics the effect of in vivo chronic systemic exposure to a soluble NMDAR antagonist, producing a block of activity-dependent remodeling of retinotectal projections.
source: These results demonstrate that extended photo-antagonism of LiGluN2A(G712C) mimics the effect of in vivo chronic systemic exposure to a soluble NMDAR antagonist, producing a block of activity-dependent remodeling of retinotectal projections.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings reported in the results section.

claim: A family of four Light-gated GluN subunits, or LiGluNs, was engineered: a light-activated GluN2A, a light-activated GluN2B, a light-antagonized GluN2A and a light-antagonized GluN1, isoform 1a, (GluN1a).
source: We now report a novel family of four Light-gated GluN subunits, or LiGluNs: 1) a light-activated GluN2A, 2) a light-activated GluN2B, 3) a light-antagonized GluN2A and 4) a light-antagonized GluN1, isoform 1a, (GluN1a).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings reported in the discussion section.
